paras: The attempted lynching of a train crew at Smith's Mines took place on October 10, 1888, when a crowd of Black miners at Smith's mines, eight miles from Birmingham, Alabama, surrounded the crew of a Birmingham Mineral Railroad freight train, swore to lynch them and fired on their engine as they fled. The crowd had gathered after the train ran over and killed a Black woman, Clara Dickson, and the crew shoveled her remains off the track. None of the crew was hit, and the story ran in papers from New York to Kansas as a narrow escape from a "negro mob."

According to a special dispatch to the New York World, the freight train was in charge of Conductor Brantley and Engineer Brown with a crew of four men, while a Birmingham dispatch of the next day described the crew as "five white men."

On the afternoon of October 10 the train ran over Dickson, whom the dispatches described as drunk and lying across the track. Her body was ground to fragments, and members of the crew took a shovel and threw the remains from the track, into a ditch beside the road according to the Sun and the Memphis Appeal.

About 200 Black miners had witnessed the accident, and the World's correspondent wrote that many of them had been drinking and nearly all were armed. Angered by the handling of the body, they surrounded the train with pistols drawn and swore they would lynch the entire crew. While five of the miners went to a nearby store for a rope, the crew climbed onto the engine and a brakeman uncoupled it from the train. The engineer opened the throttle and ran toward Birmingham under a volley of shots that broke the cab windows but hit no one. The miners then swore, the Sun reported, to kill any of the crew who ran a train past the mines again.

The only follow-up in the fuller World account concerned the railroad: the superintendent told the crew that the first man to talk to the newspapers would lose his job, though some had already decided to seek work on another road. The last item found, a brief in the Charlotte Messenger on October 20, said only that the crew escaped on their train; no report of arrests, of an inquest into Dickson's death or of any prosecution was found.

The story reached the press through at least three differently worded Birmingham dispatches, all told from the crew's side; no account from the miners appears. The New York Sun ran it on October 11 as "A Mob of Negroes Threatened to Lynch a Railroad Crew," and the Washington Evening Star printed the World special under "Wanted to Lynch the Crew," with a deck on railroad men who "barely escaped from the negro mob." The Clarksville Evening Chronicle headed its own version "Negro Riot in Alabama."

The October 11 dispatch put race in its first line, saying 200 "negro miners" had made "a desperate attempt to lynch five white men," and the Memphis Appeal headed it "Furious Negroes." The same text ran in the Indianapolis Journal as "Cheating a Mob of Lynchers" and in the Telegram-Herald under a deck that read "Railroad Men Shovel a Bleeding Body Into the Ditch." Several versions also dwelt on the treatment of the body, the Appeal writing that the crew "dumped the still bleeding flesh of the woman into a ditch."
Weeklies carried both versions through October 18, from the Emporia Weekly News and the Middleburgh Post ("A Close Call") to the Butler Weekly Times ("A Narrow Escape From Lynching").

The Clarksville Evening Chronicle printed a sharply different account, putting the crowd at 1,500 and the accident at noon. In its version the crowd charged the trainmen when they tried to remove the remains, threw stones, fired several shots and cried "Let's lynch the murderers" as two men brought a rope, whereas the other dispatches gave about 200 miners and placed the shooting after the engine pulled away.
Smaller details also varied: the Maysville Evening Bulletin called the woman "Cora Dickson," and the fuller World text named the engineer as both Brown and Lawson.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of a train crew at Smith's Mines
bases: A crowd of Black miners surrounded a freight crew, swore to lynch them, sent for a rope and fired on their fleeing engine (A1, A2, A5); no one was killed, so this is an attempted lynching.

No one was killed by the crowd: the crew escaped and none was hit (A1, A5); the only death, Clara Dickson's, was caused by the train (A1, A2). The crowd of about 200 (A1) acted without authority and, in one version, called the crew 'murderers' (A3), so this was an attempted lynching.

At least three separately worded Birmingham dispatches (A1, A2/A4, A3, A5) agree on the train death, the crowd's threat to lynch the crew, the rope and the shots at the escaping engine, though all appear to come from the railroad side.

accounts.label: Birmingham dispatch to the New York Sun
accounts.gist: 200 negro miners, angered by the crew shoveling the body into a ditch, surrounded the train and sent for a rope; the crew fled on the engine under a storm of bullets, and the miners swore to kill them if they returned.

accounts.label: New York World special
accounts.gist: Many miners were drinking and nearly all armed; they drew pistols and swore to lynch the crew, and while five went for a rope a brakeman uncoupled the engine; the fuller text adds that the engineer did not slacken speed and that the superintendent threatened the crew's jobs.

accounts.label: Clarksville Evening Chronicle version
accounts.gist: 1,500 negroes gathered at noon, charged the trainmen when they tried to remove the remains, threw stones, fired shots and cried 'Let's lynch the murderers' as two brought a rope.

accounts.label: Birmingham dispatch of Oct. 11
accounts.gist: 200 negro miners made a 'desperate attempt' to lynch five white men after the crew dumped the woman's 'still bleeding flesh' into a ditch; bullets broke the cab windows.

framing.detail: The Sun headed it 'A Mob of Negroes Threatened to Lynch a Railroad Crew' and the Evening Star 'Wanted to Lynch the Crew' with a deck on the 'negro mob'.
The Oct. 11 dispatch led with 200 negro miners trying 'to lynch five white men' under 'Furious Negroes', yet stressed the crew dumping the 'still bleeding flesh' into a ditch.
The Clarksville Evening Chronicle headed its version 'Negro Riot in Alabama' and noted the leaders were drunk.
